A sextant is a handheld navigational instrument used to measure the angle between a celestial object — such as the sun, the moon, or a star — and the horizon. That angle, once known, tells a navigator exactly where on Earth they are standing (or sailing).

Imagine you're on a ship in the middle of the ocean with no land in sight — no roads, no signs, no landmarks. How do you know where you are? The answer lies in the sky.

The key insight behind the sextant is this: the height of the sun (or a star) above the horizon changes depending on where you are on Earth. If you're near the equator, the noon sun is almost directly overhead. The further north or south you travel, the lower the sun sits in the sky. This isn't random — it follows precise, predictable geometry. So if you can measure exactly how high the sun is above the horizon at a specific moment, you can reverse-engineer your position.

That's precisely what a sextant lets you do — measure that angle with great accuracy.

A sextant is roughly the shape of a slice of pie (a fan or wedge). It's small enough to hold in one hand. Its main parts are:

  • A telescope or sighting tube — you look through this at the horizon.
  • Two mirrors — these work together to reflect the image of the sun (or star) into your line of sight.
  • A curved, graduated arc — this is the bottom edge of the "slice," marked off in degrees, like a protractor. It spans 60 degrees of arc.
  • A moveable arm — this swings along the arc and lets you adjust the angle you're measuring. You read the angle off the arc where this arm points.
  • Shaded filters — dark glass filters you flip in front of the mirrors so you can safely look in the direction of the bright sun without damaging your eyes.

The cleverest feature of the sextant is its use of mirrors. When you look through the telescope, you see two images at once:

  1. The real horizon, seen directly through part of the telescope.
  2. The reflected image of the sun (or star), bounced into your view via the two mirrors.

By moving the arm along the arc, you adjust the mirrors until the reflected image of the sun appears to touch the horizon — as if the sun is sitting right on the edge of the sea. The angle at which the arm sits when these two images are aligned is the angle you wanted: the altitude of the sun above the horizon.

This technique — using mirrors to bring two separate images into alignment — is elegant because it lets you measure the angle precisely even on a rocking, pitching ship. Both images move together when the ship moves, so they stay aligned regardless of the vessel's motion. This was a major improvement over earlier instruments.
What You Do With That Angle

Measuring the angle is only step one. The real goal is figuring out your position, and that takes a bit more:

To find latitude (how far north or south you are):
You measure the angle of the sun at exactly noon — the moment it's at its highest point in the sky. Using that angle alongside known tables (called nautical almanacs, which list where celestial bodies are at every moment of every day), you can calculate your latitude. This was well understood by navigators for centuries.

To find longitude (how far east or west you are):
This is trickier. You need an accurate clock — called a marine chronometer — set to a reference time zone (historically, Greenwich, England). By measuring the sun's or a star's angle at a precise known time, and comparing it to where that object should be at that time according to the almanac, you can work out your longitude too.

Together, latitude and longitude tell you exactly where on Earth you are. A skilled navigator using a sextant and a reliable chronometer can pin down their position to within about 1–2 nautical miles, which is roughly 2–3 kilometers. For centuries, this was astonishing accuracy.

Before the sextant and before reliable clocks, ocean navigation was extremely dangerous and imprecise. Sailors could estimate latitude reasonably well using simpler instruments, but longitude was notoriously difficult. Ships ran aground, got lost, and took wildly inefficient routes because they simply didn't know where they were east-to-west.

The sextant (which became widely used in the mid-1700s, refining earlier instruments) changed all of this. Combined with accurate clocks, it gave sailors a reliable, repeatable method for knowing their precise position anywhere on Earth. It was the GPS of its era — arguably one of the most important technologies in the history of exploration, trade, and warfare. It enabled European powers to chart and cross every ocean with confidence, opened up global trade routes, and made world maps far more accurate.

Yes, though far less commonly for primary navigation. GPS has largely replaced it. But the sextant has not disappeared:

  • Maritime law and training — professional sailors and naval officers in many countries are still required to learn celestial navigation with a sextant. If your electronics fail in the middle of the ocean, you need a backup.
  • Backup navigation — a sextant requires no batteries, no satellites, no internet, and no electricity. It is completely self-sufficient. As long as you can see the sky, it works.
  • Traditional and solo sailing — many long-distance and solo sailors still use sextants either out of necessity, tradition, or personal preference.
  • Military — naval forces retain the skill as a fallback in case of electronic warfare or equipment failure.
  • Astronomy and surveying — specialized versions are used in certain professional applications.

A sextant is a precision optical instrument that measures the angle between the sun (or another celestial body) and the horizon. That angle, combined with the exact time and published astronomical tables, tells you where you are on Earth. It was the cornerstone of ocean navigation for roughly 250 years and remains a symbol of seamanship, precision engineering, and human ingenuity in finding one's way across a featureless sea using nothing but the sky above.
